# From Direct Sampling to Markov Chains {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

- [When direct sampling is difficult](#when-direct-sampling-is-difficult)
- [The Markov property](#the-markov-property)
- [Examples of Markov chains](#examples-of-markov-chains)

## When direct sampling is difficult {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

- Quantile, affine, and exact transport maps
    - [Global construction]{.alert}: a map that produces the target distribution
- Acceptance–rejection
    - [Global bound]{.alert}: a proposal envelope valid throughout the target support
- [Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)]{.alert}, via Metropolis–Hastings
    - [Local decision]{.alert}: density ratios at the current and proposed states
    - No global envelope; proposed moves need not be nearby

::: {.key-point}
From a global sampling construction to a [target-preserving transition]{.alert}

Under suitable conditions, the distribution of $X_i$ approaches the target as $i\to\infty$
:::

## The Markov property {data-state="goldborder" .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="probability"}

Let $\mathcal X$ be the state space for $X_0,X_1,\ldots$

The sequence is a [Markov chain]{.alert} when, for every measurable $A\subseteq\mathcal X$,

\begin{equation*}
\Prob(X_{i+1}\in A\mid X_i=x_i,\ldots,X_0=x_0)\\
=\Prob(X_{i+1}\in A\mid X_i=x_i)
\end{equation*}

[Where the chain goes next depends only on where it is now]{.alert}, not on how it arrived

We are interested in the [asymptotic behavior of $X_i$]{.alert}

- In MCMC, construct the chain so that, under suitable conditions, the
  [distribution of $X_i$ approaches the target]{.alert} as $i\to\infty$

## Examples of Markov chains {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="probability"}

Assume $Z_0,Z_1,\ldots\ \IIDsim\ \Norm(0,1)$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Markov

\begin{align*}
X_0&=0,& X_{i+1}&=X_i+Z_i\\
X_0&=0,& X_{i+1}&=i+Z_i
\end{align*}

The second chain is [not time homogeneous]{.alert}: its transition law changes with $i$
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Not Markov as written

$$
X_0=X_1=0,
\qquad X_{i+1}=X_{i-1}+Z_i
$$

The pair $Y_i=(X_{i-1},X_i)$ [is Markov]{.alert} because its state retains the needed history
:::
:::

Only the first is a [martingale]{.alert}: its expected next value, given the history, equals its current value

# Metropolis–Hastings Sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

- [The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm](#the-metropolishastings-algorithm)
- [Why the acceptance ratio works](#why-the-acceptance-ratio-works)
- [The Metropolis algorithm](#the-metropolis-algorithm)
- [Metropolis practice](#metropolis-practice)
- [A random-walk Metropolis example](#a-random-walk-metropolis-example)
- [Separated modes can trap a chain](#separated-modes-can-trap-a-chain)
- [Tuning and diagnostics](#tuning-and-diagnostics)

## The Metropolis–Hastings algorithm {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

Suppose

- the target has known, possibly unnormalized density
  $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$
- $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z\mid x)$ proposes a new state $z$ from the
  current state $x$

Given $X_0$, repeat for $i=0,\ldots,n-1$:

1. Generate $Z\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\cdot\mid X_i)$ and
   $U\sim\Unif[0,1]$
2. Compute

   $$
   \alpha(X_i,Z)=\min\!\left\{1,
   \frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(Z)\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(X_i\mid Z)}
   {\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(X_i)\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(Z\mid X_i)}\right\}
   =\min\!\left\{1,
\frac{\text{joint density of first $Z$, then $X_i$}}
{\text{joint density of first $X_i$, then $Z$}}\right\}
   $$

3. Set $X_{i+1}=Z$ if $U\le\alpha(X_i,Z)$<br>Otherwise set
   $X_{i+1}=X_i$

[Every iteration accepts either the proposal or the current state]{.alert}<br>Nothing is discarded


## Why the acceptance ratio works {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="probability"}

The ratio compares the two directions of a proposed transition:

$$
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(Z)\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(X_i\mid Z)}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(X_i)\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(Z\mid X_i)}
=
\frac{\text{target weight at $Z$}\times\text{return proposal}}
{\text{target weight at $X_i$}\times\text{forward proposal}}
$$

- Moves toward higher target density are favored
- Asymmetric proposals are corrected by the proposal-density ratio
- The normalizing constant in $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$ cancels

::: {.key-point}
The transition kernel satisfies [detailed balance]{.alert} with the target distribution, making the target invariant under suitable conditions
:::

## The Metropolis algorithm {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

If the proposal is symmetric,

$$
\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z\mid x)
=\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(x\mid z),
$$

then the acceptance probability simplifies to

$$
\alpha(x,z)=\min\!\left\{1,
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(z)}{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)}\right\}
$$

For a random-walk proposal $Z=X_i+\epsilon_i$ with symmetric $\epsilon_i$:

- accept every move to a state with at least as much target density
- accept some downhill moves, which keeps the chain from becoming trapped immediately
- repeat $X_i$ when a proposal is rejected

## Metropolis practice {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="practice"}

Use the uniform numbers in order and choose a random order of the candidate $x$ values

| $i$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $U_i$ | 0.6 | 0.1 | 0.3 | 0.5 | 0.9 | 0.2 | 0.1 | 0.4 |

| $x$ | $-1.2$ | $-0.8$ | $-0.5$ | $0.6$ | $1.1$ | $1.4$ | $2.0$ | $2.2$ |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)$ | 0.1 | 0.8 | 2.0 | 1.6 | 0.5 | 2.6 | 2.4 | 1.0 |

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Starting at $x=-1.2$, follow several Metropolis steps and record each accepted or repeated state</span>
:::

## A random-walk Metropolis example {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

Target a bimodal Gaussian mixture using the symmetric proposal

$$
Z\mid X_i=x\sim\Norm(x,1.4^2)
$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Random-walk Metropolis example with the bimodal target density, sampled-state histogram, and Markov-chain trace"
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| out-width: 98%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "stix"
rng = np.random.default_rng(56503)

def target_density(x):
    return 0.35 * norm.pdf(x, -2.2, 0.65) + 0.65 * norm.pdf(x, 1.4, 0.9)

n_steps = 12000
chain = np.empty(n_steps)
chain[0] = 0.0
accepted = 0
for i in range(n_steps - 1):
    proposal = chain[i] + rng.normal(0, 1.4)
    ratio = target_density(proposal) / target_density(chain[i])
    if rng.random() <= min(1.0, ratio):
        chain[i + 1] = proposal
        accepted += 1
    else:
        chain[i + 1] = chain[i]

burn = 1500
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 700)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 5.6), constrained_layout=True)
axes[0].hist(chain[burn:], bins=55, density=True, color="#9bc8c6",
             edgecolor="white", label="MCMC sample")
axes[0].plot(x, target_density(x), color="#1f5a91", linewidth=3,
             label="target density")
axes[0].set_xlabel(r"$x$", fontsize=20, math_fontfamily="stix")
axes[0].set_ylabel("density", fontsize=17)
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=14)
axes[1].plot(np.arange(500), chain[burn:burn + 500], color="#1f5a91", linewidth=1.4)
axes[1].set_xlabel("iteration", fontsize=17)
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$X_i$", fontsize=20, math_fontfamily="stix")
axes[1].set_title(f"acceptance rate = {accepted / (n_steps - 1):.2f}", fontsize=16)
for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=13)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.16)
plt.show()
```

## Separated modes can trap a chain {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

Same mixture weights and widths; move the means to $-5$ and $5$<br>
Keep $Z\mid X_i=x\sim\Norm(x,1.4^2)$; start one chain in each mode

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "Two Metropolis chains started in opposite, widely separated Gaussian modes remain in their starting modes, despite moderate acceptance rates"
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| out-width: 95%

from scipy.special import logsumexp

def separated_log_density(x):
    return logsumexp([
        np.log(0.35) + norm.logpdf(x, -5.0, 0.65),
        np.log(0.65) + norm.logpdf(x, 5.0, 0.9),
    ], axis=0)

separated_rng = np.random.default_rng(565031)
separated_runs = []
for initial in (-5.0, 5.0):
    states = np.empty(12000)
    states[0] = initial
    log_current = separated_log_density(initial)
    n_accept = 0
    for i in range(len(states) - 1):
        candidate = states[i] + separated_rng.normal(0, 1.4)
        log_candidate = separated_log_density(candidate)
        if np.log(separated_rng.random()) <= min(0.0, log_candidate - log_current):
            states[i + 1] = candidate
            log_current = log_candidate
            n_accept += 1
        else:
            states[i + 1] = states[i]
    separated_runs.append((initial, states, n_accept / (len(states) - 1)))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.4), constrained_layout=True)
grid = np.linspace(-8, 8, 800)
axes[0].plot(grid, np.exp(separated_log_density(grid)), color="#1f5a91",
             linewidth=3, label="target density")
for (initial, states, rate), color in zip(separated_runs, ["#228833", "#cc6677"]):
    retained = states[1500:]
    crossings = np.count_nonzero(np.diff(states > 0))
    axes[0].hist(retained, bins=np.linspace(-8, 8, 90), density=True,
                 histtype="step", linewidth=2, color=color,
                 label=rf"start $X_0={initial:g}$")
    axes[1].plot(np.arange(len(states)), states, color=color, linewidth=0.6,
                 label=f"accept {rate:.0%}; crossings {crossings}")
axes[0].set_xlabel(r"$x$", fontsize=20, math_fontfamily="stix")
axes[0].set_ylabel("density", fontsize=17)
axes[1].set_xlabel("iteration", fontsize=17)
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$X_i$", fontsize=20, math_fontfamily="stix")
axes[1].axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.8, linestyle="--")
for ax in axes:
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=12)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=12)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

[Acceptance within a mode does not establish exploration of both modes]{.alert}

## Tuning and diagnostics {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="statistics"}

MCMC is attractive because it

- samples from complicated, unnormalized target densities
- is often straightforward to implement

The proposal and starting point require care:

- proposals that are too small explore slowly and produce highly dependent samples
- proposals that are too large have low acceptance rates and many repeats
- multimodal targets may trap a single chain in one mode

Useful responses include [pilot runs]{.alert}, [multiple chains]{.alert}, and [parallel tempering]{.alert}

[`MetropolisHastings` companion notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/sampling/MetropolisHastings.ipynb)

::: {.key-point}
Diagnose both [exploration]{.alert} of the full state space and [concentration]{.alert} in high-density regions
:::

# Kernel Discrepancy {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

- [How can we measure sample quality?](#how-can-we-measure-sample-quality)
- [What discrepancy measures](#what-discrepancy-measures)
- [Symmetric positive definite kernels](#symmetric-positive-definite-kernels)
- [Discrepancy between distributions](#discrepancy-between-distributions)
- [Empirical distributions](#empirical-distributions)
- [Unbiased estimates of squared discrepancy](#unbiased-estimates-of-squared-discrepancy)
- [Relative entropy: another comparison](#relative-entropy-another-comparison)
- [Stein discrepancy](#stein-discrepancy)
- [Comparing distribution discrepancies](#comparing-distribution-discrepancies)

## How can we measure sample quality? {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

For samples $\{x_i\}_{i=0}^{m-1}$ and $\{z_j\}_{j=0}^{n-1}$, a kernel $K$ defines

\begin{align*}
D^2\!\left(\{x_i\}_{i=0}^{m-1},\{z_j\}_{j=0}^{n-1};K\right)
&=\frac{1}{m^2}\sum_{i,j=0}^{m-1}K(x_i,x_j)\\
&\quad-\frac{2}{mn}\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}K(x_i,z_j)
+\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}K(z_i,z_j)
\end{align*}

- Also called [maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)]{.alert} in machine learning
- Direct computation requires $\Order(\max(m,n)^2)$ kernel evaluations
- The answer depends on the chosen kernel and its parameters

## What discrepancy measures {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

Kernel discrepancy measures

- the difference between two probability distributions
- the [worst-case integration error]{.alert} over the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space
- the [root mean squared integration error]{.alert} when the integrand is modeled as a Gaussian process with covariance kernel $K$

[`Discrepancy` companion notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/performance/Discrepancy.ipynb)

Tutorial: [{{< meta papers.hickirsor_2026_qmc_tutorial.short >}}]({{< meta papers.hickirsor_2026_qmc_tutorial.arxiv_url >}}), Section 5 — kernel discrepancy and integration error

::: {.key-point}
The kernel determines which differences between distributions matter most
:::

::: {.notes}
{{< meta papers.hickirsor_2026_qmc_tutorial.full >}}

Section 5.1 develops kernel-defined discrepancy and worst-case error;
Section 5.2 treats centered discrepancy; Section 5.5 connects randomized
and Bayesian error. These supplement Owen's Chapter 15 and provide a direct
reference for the kernel-based presentation in this deck. The tutorial's
unit-cube formulation is extended here to general target distributions.
:::

## Symmetric positive definite kernels {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="statistics"}

A kernel $K:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\reals$ is [symmetric positive definite]{.alert} when every Gram matrix

$$
\mK=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=0}^{n-1}
$$

is symmetric positive definite for distinct $x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}$

Examples include

\begin{align*}
K(t,x)&=\exp\!\left(-\norm{t-x}^2/h^2\right),
&&\mathcal X=\reals^d,\\
K(t,x)&=\prod_{\ell=1}^d\left[1+\frac{\gamma_\ell^2}{2}
\left(\abs{t_\ell-\tfrac12}+\abs{x_\ell-\tfrac12}-\abs{t_\ell-x_\ell}\right)\right],
&&\mathcal X=[0,1]^d
\end{align*}

- First is a squared exponential kernel; second yields centered discrepancy

- Kernels usually have [parameters]{.alert} to be chosen or estimated

## Discrepancy between distributions {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

For independent $X,X'\sim F_X$ and $Z,Z'\sim F_Z$,

\begin{align*}
D^2(F_X,F_Z;K)
&=\Ex[K(X,X')]-2\Ex[K(X,Z)]+\Ex[K(Z,Z')]\\
&=\int_{\mathcal X^2}K(x,x')\,\dif(F_X-F_Z)(x)\,\dif(F_X-F_Z)(x')\\
&\ge0
\end{align*}

If both distributions have densities,

$$
D^2(F_X,F_Z;K)
=\int_{\mathcal X^2}K(x,x')
\{\varrho_X(x)-\varrho_Z(x)\}
\{\varrho_X(x')-\varrho_Z(x')\}\,\dif x\,\dif x'
$$

## Empirical distributions {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

For the empirical distribution of $z_0,\ldots,z_{n-1}$,

\begin{align*}
D^2(F_X,\{z_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)
&=\int_{\mathcal X^2}K(x,x')\,\dif F_X(x)\,\dif F_X(x')\\
&\quad-\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\int_{\mathcal X}K(x,z_i)\,\dif F_X(x)\\
&\quad+\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}K(z_i,z_j)
\end{align*}

The same formula covers [one target distribution and one sample]{.alert} or [two samples]{.alert}

## Unbiased estimates of squared discrepancy {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="statistics"}

The squared discrepancy is nonnegative

But an unbiased estimator [may be negative]{.alert}

Replace within-sample sums by off-diagonal averages:

\begin{align*}
D_{\mathrm{unb}}^2\!\left(\{x_i\}_{i=0}^{m-1},\{z_j\}_{j=0}^{n-1};K\right)
&=\frac{1}{m(m-1)}\sum_{\substack{i,j=0\\i\ne j}}^{m-1}K(x_i,x_j)\\
&\quad-\frac{2}{mn}\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}K(x_i,z_j)
+\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{\substack{i,j=0\\i\ne j}}^{n-1}K(z_i,z_j)
\end{align*}

[Unbiased]{.alert} describes the estimator's expectation, not the sign of each realization

A more negative realization is [not a better match]{.alert}; it is a larger downward sampling fluctuation

---

### What does unbiased mean?

::: {.exitem .roman}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>
Let $\{X_i\}_{i=0}^{m-1}$ and $\{Z_j\}_{j=0}^{n-1}$ be independent IID samples from $F_X$ and $F_Z$
<span class="exsub">Take expectations term by term to show $\Ex[D_{\mathrm{unb}}^2]=D^2(F_X,F_Z;K)$</span>
<span class="exsub">What is the expectation when $F_X=F_Z$?</span>
<span class="exsub">Why may a realization be negative, and does more negative mean a better match?</span>
<span class="exsub">Which step fails when the $X_i$ are successive Metropolis states?</span>
</span>
:::

## Relative entropy: another comparison {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="statistics"}

[Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence]{.alert}, also called [relative entropy]{.alert}

For normalized densities $\varrho_X$ and $\varrho_Z$,

\begin{align*}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(F_X\Vert F_Z)
&=\int_{\mathcal X}\varrho_X(x)
\log\!\left(\frac{\varrho_X(x)}{\varrho_Z(x)}\right)\,\dif x
\end{align*}

- Nonnegative; zero exactly when the distributions agree
- Generally asymmetric; infinite if $F_X$ assigns mass where $F_Z$ assigns none
- Entropy describes one distribution; [relative entropy compares two]{.alert}
- Variational inference fits an approximate density by minimizing KL to the target

::: {.key-point}
Finite empirical sample versus continuous target: KL is infinite

Kernel discrepancy compares these directly, without density estimation
:::

::: {.notes}
Use natural logarithms and the convention that a zero numerator contributes
zero. The density formula assumes a common dominating measure. More generally,
KL is infinite unless the first distribution is absolutely continuous with
respect to the second. A finite empirical measure and an atomless target are
mutually singular, so both KL directions are infinite; density estimation or
binning changes the comparison. This does not prevent studying KL convergence
of a chain's marginal law, which is distinct from its empirical measure.

Variational inference commonly minimizes
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(F_{\mathrm{approx}}\Vert F_{\mathrm{tar}})$ over a tractable
family. It is an optimization alternative to MCMC, not itself an MCMC sampler.
An unknown target normalizing constant contributes an additive constant to
this objective; it does not prevent optimization, but is needed for its
absolute numerical value.

References: [Shalizi, Information Theory I, entropy and divergence](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/dm/20/lectures/09/lecture-09.html#entropy-log-likelihood-divergence);
[Blei, Kucukelbir, and McAuliffe, Variational Inference: A Review for Statisticians](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00670)
:::

## Stein discrepancy {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="statistics"}

For a smooth positive target density $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)=\widetilde\varrho(x)/C$,
the [score]{.alert} removes the unknown normalizing constant

\begin{align*}
s(x)&=\nabla_x\log\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)
=\nabla_x\log\widetilde\varrho(x)\\
\mathcal T g(x)&=s(x)^\mathsf{T}g(x)+\nabla\!\cdot g(x),
\qquad \Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[\mathcal T g(X)]=0
\end{align*}

- Stein discrepancy: largest sample violation of this identity over a chosen class of $g$
- [Kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD)]{.alert}: use a vector-valued RKHS unit ball
- Computable from candidate points, target scores, and kernel derivatives
- No target reference sample or normalizing constant required

::: {.key-point}
Requires smoothness and valid boundary conditions; kernel choice matters

Some KSDs fail to detect nonconvergence; separated-mode weights can be hard to assess
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide describes the common Langevin, score-based Stein operator for a
continuous target, not every Stein discrepancy. Here $g$ is a vector field;
the identity follows by integration by parts when the boundary term vanishes
and the expectations exist. On bounded supports, the function class or operator
must enforce the appropriate boundary conditions. Discrete targets require a
different operator.

For candidate points $x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}$, the discrepancy is
$\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}|n^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathcal T g(x_i)|$.
Applying Stein operators to both arguments of a sufficiently smooth base kernel
gives a target-dependent Stein kernel and a pairwise-sum formula for KSD squared.
Thus KSD is closely related to MMD, using a specially constructed kernel whose
target expectation vanishes. It is not a wholly unrelated alternative to
kernel discrepancy. Direct pairwise computation is quadratic in sample size.

Suitable kernels and target assumptions give convergence-determining KSDs;
the failure of some kernels is not a universal failure of Stein discrepancy.
Weak sensitivity to weights of well-separated modes is a finite-sample testing
limitation, distinct from an asymptotic convergence theorem.

References: [Liu, Lee, and Jordan (2016)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v48/liub16.html);
[Gorham and Mackey (2017)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/gorham17a.html);
[Liu, Duncan, and Gandy (2023)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/liu23i.html)
:::

## Comparing distribution discrepancies

| | Ordinary MMD | KL / relative entropy | Score-based KSD |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Normalizing constant | Direct integrals: needed; reference samples: not needed | Value: generally needed; optimization: may drop out | Cancels from the score |
| Benefit | Sample comparisons; integration-error meaning | Information-theoretic meaning; variational fitting | No target draws or normalizer |
| Limitation | Kernel choice; target integration or reference error | Asymmetry; empirical vs continuous: infinite | Derivatives; boundary, kernel, and mode sensitivity |

With $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}=\widetilde\varrho/C$ and approximation density $\varrho_{\mathrm{approx}}$,

\begin{align*}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(F_{\mathrm{approx}}\Vert F_{\mathrm{tar}})
&=\Ex_{\mathrm{approx}}\!\left[\log\!\left(
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{approx}}(X)}{\widetilde\varrho(X)}\right)\right]+\log C
\end{align*}

[Fixed target]{.alert}: $\log C$ does not affect minimization over the approximation

::: {.notes}
The MMD row concerns ordinary kernels, before the Stein construction. Direct
target integration requires normalized expectations, although a constant may
already be incorporated in an analytic kernel mean or removed by computing a
ratio of integrals. Empirical two-sample MMD itself never evaluates a density;
obtaining trustworthy target reference draws may still be difficult. In this
course, the discrepancy notebook uses independent acceptance--rejection draws
as its reference, so the MMD calculation does not use a normalizing constant.

The KL optimization statement is for a fixed target and the displayed direction.
It is not permission to omit a parameter-dependent normalizer when fitting
the target model. Density or density-ratio estimators can estimate KL from
samples, but that differs from plugging an atomic empirical measure into KL.

The comparisons concern different quantities; their numerical magnitudes are
not interchangeable, and none is automatically a calibrated MCMC stopping rule.
References are given in the preceding KL and Stein slide notes.
:::

# Discrepancy as Integration Error {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

- [A reproducing kernel Hilbert space](#a-reproducing-kernel-hilbert-space)
- [Worst-case integration error](#worst-case-integration-error)
- [The discrepancy identity](#the-discrepancy-identity)
- [Average-case integration error](#average-case-integration-error)
- [What the kernel controls](#what-the-kernel-controls)
- [Centered discrepancy and smoothness](#centered-discrepancy-and-smoothness)

## A reproducing kernel Hilbert space {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="statistics"}

Every symmetric positive definite kernel $K$ defines a Hilbert space $\mathcal H_K$ of functions on $\mathcal X$ with the [reproducing property]{.alert}

$$
f(x)=\langle K(\cdot,x),f\rangle_{\mathcal H_K}
$$

Assume $\int_{\mathcal X^2}K(x,x')\,\dif F_X(x)\,\dif F_X(x')$ is finite

Then both

\begin{align*}
f&\longmapsto\int_{\mathcal X}f(x)\,\dif F_X(x),\\
f&\longmapsto\int_{\mathcal X}f(x)\,\dif F_X(x)-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(z_i)
\end{align*}

are bounded linear functionals on $\mathcal H_K$

## Worst-case integration error {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

By the Riesz representation theorem, some $\zeta\in\mathcal H_K$ satisfies

$$
\int_{\mathcal X}f(x)\,\dif F_X(x)-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(z_i)
=\langle\zeta,f\rangle_{\mathcal H_K}
$$

Therefore, by Cauchy–Schwarz,

$$
\left\lvert\int_{\mathcal X}f(x)\,\dif F_X(x)-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(z_i)\right\rvert
\le\norm{\zeta}_{\mathcal H_K}\norm{f}_{\mathcal H_K}
$$

This separates [sample quality]{.alert}, $\norm{\zeta}_{\mathcal H_K}$, from [integrand difficulty]{.alert}, $\norm{f}_{\mathcal H_K}$

## The discrepancy identity {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

The representer is

$$
\zeta(x')=\int_{\mathcal X}K(x,x')\,\dif F_X(x)
-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}K(z_i,x')
$$

Its squared norm is exactly the squared discrepancy:

\begin{align*}
\norm{\zeta}_{\mathcal H_K}^2
&=\int_{\mathcal X^2}K(x,x')\,\dif F_X(x)\,\dif F_X(x')\\
&\quad-\frac2n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\int_{\mathcal X}K(x,z_i)\,\dif F_X(x)
+\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}K(z_i,z_j)\\
&=D^2(F_X,\{z_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)
\end{align*}

Thus discrepancy is the [worst-case error over $\norm{f}_{\mathcal H_K}\le1$]{.alert}

## Average-case integration error {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="statistics"}

Suppose $f$ is modeled as a zero-mean Gaussian process with covariance kernel $K$

For deterministic $z_0,\ldots,z_{n-1}$,

\begin{align*}
&\Ex_f\!\left[
\left\{\int_{\mathcal X}f(x)\,\dif F_X(x)-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(z_i)\right\}^2
\right]\\
&\quad=\int_{\mathcal X^2}K(x,x')\,\dif F_X(x)\,\dif F_X(x')
-\frac2n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\int_{\mathcal X}K(x,z_i)\,\dif F_X(x)
+\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}K(z_i,z_j)\\
&\quad=D^2(F_X,\{z_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)
\end{align*}

Discrepancy is also the [root mean squared error under the Gaussian-process model]{.alert}

## What the kernel controls {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="statistics"}

- The numerical value of discrepancy depends on $K$ and its hyperparameters
- Multiplying $K$ by $c^2$ multiplies discrepancy by $\abs{c}$
- Kernel structure encodes assumptions about
  - domain and smoothness
  - periodicity
  - coordinate importance
- In the average-case setting, hyperparameters may be estimated by empirical Bayes or maximum likelihood

For IID $Z_i\sim F_X$,

$$
\Ex\!\left[D^2(F_X,\{Z_i\}_{i=0}^{n-1};K)\right]
=\frac1n\left\{
\int K(x,x)\,\dif F_X(x)-\int K(x,x')\,\dif F_X(x)\,\dif F_X(x')
\right\}
$$

## Centered discrepancy and smoothness {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

For $\mathcal X=[0,1]^d$, the centered-discrepancy kernel is

$$
K(t,x)=\prod_{\ell=1}^d\left[1+\frac{\gamma_\ell^2}{2}
\left(\abs{t_\ell-\tfrac12}+\abs{x_\ell-\tfrac12}-\abs{t_\ell-x_\ell}\right)\right]
$$

Its norm combines the function value at the center with weighted square-integrals of mixed derivatives:

\begin{align*}
\norm{f}_{\mathcal H_K}^2
&=\abs{f(1/2,\ldots,1/2)}^2
+\norm{\frac{\partial f(x_1,1/2,\ldots)}{\gamma_1\partial x_1}}_2^2\\
&\quad+\norm{\frac{\partial^2 f(x_1,x_2,1/2,\ldots)}
{\gamma_1\gamma_2\partial x_1\partial x_2}}_2^2
+\cdots
+\norm{\frac{\partial^d f(x)}
{\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_d\partial x_1\cdots\partial x_d}}_2^2
\end{align*}

The weights $\gamma_\ell$ express [coordinate importance]{.alert}

- [Direct sampling, MCMC, and event simulation](#direct-sampling-mcmc-and-event-simulation)
- [Maximum likelihood estimation](#maximum-likelihood-estimation)
- [Bayesian inference](#bayesian-inference)
- [Queueing systems](#queueing-systems)

## Direct sampling, MCMC, and event simulation {data-state="goldborder"}

| Application | What matters | Natural simulation approach |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Finance: European / Asian options | Finite maturity; terminal value or path average | [Direct sampling]{.alert} of model inputs → independent paths; refine time steps as needed |
| Bayesian inference | Complicated, concentrated posterior; often known only up to normalization | [MCMC]{.alert} when direct posterior sampling is difficult; mixing still matters |
| Queueing: waiting / blocking | Arrival and departure order; interactions at individual events | [Event-driven simulation]{.alert} of the system's Markov state; no fixed fine time grid |

- Finance: couple coarse and fine paths with [multilevel Monte Carlo](05-selected-topics.html#multilevel-monte-carlo) later
- Barrier options: fine path detail can matter in finance too

::: {.key-point}
Choose by [access to the distribution]{.alert} and [which details affect the answer]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
The finite horizon makes a finance path a finite collection of random inputs
after discretization; it does not by itself make direct sampling easy. In the
models used here, Gaussian increments or known transition laws are available,
so independent inputs generate independent paths, even though values within
each path are dependent and may form a Markov process. Low discrepancy inputs
are another choice, but do not give independent paths.

For geometric Brownian motion, transitions on a chosen grid can be sampled
exactly; a European terminal payoff needs no intervening time steps. A
continuously averaged Asian payoff still needs control of path-integration
error. A barrier payoff can depend critically on crossings between grid points.
Refinement and Brownian-bridge corrections address different sources of error.
Multilevel Monte Carlo combines many cheap coarse paths with fewer coupled
fine-minus-coarse corrections; it is not MCMC.

A sharp posterior alone does not require MCMC: a narrow normal or a conjugate
posterior may be sampled directly. The obstacle is the lack of an effective
direct sampler for the posterior geometry, often with only an unnormalized
density available. Narrow directions and separated modes can also impede MCMC.

Queueing belongs here as simulation of a Markov system, not as a claim that
Metropolis--Hastings is needed for queues. Event order and state-dependent
interactions determine waiting and blocking. Simulate directly from arrival
and service laws, advancing to the next event. Both finite-horizon and
steady-state questions are possible; steady-state time averages require
appropriate time weighting and attention to initialization.

Additional spoken examples: reliability simulation with directly sampled
component lifetimes; inventory systems with event-driven demand and restocking.

Reference for the multilevel preview and payoff-dependent refinement:
[Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo path simulation](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/gilesm/files/opre.pdf)
:::

## Maximum likelihood estimation {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="estimation"}

Our Monte Carlo error assessments so far have used a [frequentist perspective]{.alert}

- [Frequentist:]{.alert} assess estimators by repeated-sampling bias, variance, and coverage; no likelihood is required
- [Fisherian / likelihood:]{.alert} compare parameter values through how well they explain the observed data
- [Bayesian:]{.alert} combine a sampling model with a prior to describe posterior uncertainty

::: {.key-point}
These perspectives overlap: MLE can be assessed frequentist-wise, and Bayesian inference also uses likelihood
:::

[{{< meta references.eh.full >}}]({{< meta references.eh.url >}}), Chapters 2–4

::: {.notes}
Efron and Hastie distinguish frequentist, Fisherian, and Bayesian traditions in
[{{< meta references.eh.full >}}]({{< meta references.eh.url >}}),
Chapters 2–4. The bullets emphasize the aspects relevant to this course, rather
than giving an exhaustive account of each tradition.

Our sample means, standard errors, and confidence intervals have been evaluated
through their behavior under repeated sampling. This does not require specifying
or maximizing a parametric likelihood. For example, a central limit theorem can
justify an approximate confidence interval without assuming the observations
themselves are normal.

We now introduce likelihood to explain the ingredients of Bayesian inference.
Maximizing it is one possible use; multiplying it by a prior is another.
An MLE is not a prerequisite for Bayes.
:::

---

### Likelihood and maximum likelihood estimation

The [likelihood]{.alert} is the shared starting point for MLE and Bayesian inference

For observed data $y$ and parameter $\theta$,

$$
L(\theta;y)=\varrho_{Y\mid\theta}(y\mid\theta)
$$

- Use the sampling model's density or probability mass function; [no normality assumption]{.alert}
- Hold $y$ fixed and compare candidate parameter values $\theta$

The [maximum likelihood estimator]{.alert} selects a maximizer:

$$
\htheta_{\mathrm{MLE}}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta}L(\theta;y)
$$

::: {.key-point}
[MLE:]{.alert} maximize the likelihood for a point estimate<br>
[Bayesian inference:]{.alert} combine the same likelihood with a prior for a posterior distribution
:::

::: {.notes}
MLE is an alternative method of inference, not a required step before Bayes.
The likelihood is the precursor common to both. Frequentist inference can add
confidence intervals and other uncertainty assessments; it is not limited to
point estimation. Bayesian inference can also report point summaries.

The normal model below is one worked example, not an assumption of the general
likelihood definition. The Bayesian notebook uses a normal observation model
with known variance to make an exact posterior benchmark available.

For $Y_0,\ldots,Y_{n-1}\ \IIDsim\ \Norm(\mu,\sigma^2)$,

\begin{align*}
L(\mu,\sigma^2;y)
&=(2\mpi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\!\left[-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(y_i-\mu)^2\right],\\
\hmu_{\mathrm{MLE}}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}y_i,&
\hsigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(y_i-\hmu_{\mathrm{MLE}})^2
\end{align*}
:::

## Bayesian inference {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="prob-est"}

- Especially useful when [data are limited relative to model complexity]{.alert}
- Prior knowledge supplements the data; weak data call for checking sensitivity to the prior
- Also useful with abundant data

Keep the sampling likelihood; now add prior information about $\theta$:

\begin{align*}
\varrho_{\mathrm{post}}(\theta\mid y)
&=\frac{L(\theta;y)\varrho_{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta)}{\varrho_Y(y)}\\
&\propto L(\theta;y)\varrho_{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta)
\end{align*}

---

### Computing posterior summaries

- The evidence $\varrho_Y(y)$ depends only on the observed data
- MCMC needs only the [unnormalized posterior]{.alert}
- Posterior samples estimate means, quantiles, credible intervals, and other summaries
- Optimization of the unnormalized posterior yields a maximum a posteriori estimate

::: {.key-point}
Bayesian inference is a primary reason to sample from complicated unnormalized densities
:::

[`BayesianMCMC` companion notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/applications/BayesianMCMC.ipynb)

## Queueing systems {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="probability"}

Consider a single-server queue observed at event times

\begin{align*}
A_i&=\text{time until the next arrival},\\
N_i&=\text{number of customers in the system},\\
S_i&=\text{remaining service time}
\end{align*}

Draw full interarrival times from $F_A$ and full service times from $F_S$

Residual times generally have different laws

The state $(A_i,N_i,S_i)$ is Markov when new interarrival and service durations are independent

At each event, either

- the next customer arrives before service finishes, or
- the current service finishes before the next arrival

---

### Event-driven queue simulation

```text
Initialize A[0] ~ F_A, N[0] = 0, S[0] = infinity
while the stopping rule is not met:
    if N[i] == 0:
        advance to the next arrival
        N[i+1] = 1
        generate S[i+1] ~ F_S and A[i+1] ~ F_A
    elif A[i] < S[i]:
        advance to the next arrival
        N[i+1] = N[i] + 1
        S[i+1] = S[i] - A[i]
        generate A[i+1] ~ F_A
    else:
        advance to the next service completion
        N[i+1] = N[i] - 1
        A[i+1] = A[i] - S[i]
        if N[i+1] > 0: generate S[i+1] ~ F_S
        else: S[i+1] = infinity
```

[Events replace fixed time steps]{.alert}, avoiding work when nothing changes

[Queue simulation companion notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/applications/QueueSimulation.ipynb)

---

### Tracking customer time

Add

\begin{align*}
T_i&=\text{total elapsed time},\\
W_j&=\text{waiting plus service time for customer $j$}
\end{align*}

At an arrival after elapsed time $\Delta t$:

- add $\Delta t$ to every customer currently in the system
- initialize the arriving customer's clock
- update the queue length and residual event times

At a service completion:

- add the completed service interval to all waiting customers
- record the departing customer's $W_j$
- begin service for the next customer

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Which state variables are needed if service times are not memoryless?</span>
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder" .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="prob-stat-est"}

- A Markov chain's next-state law depends on its [current state]{.alert}
- Metropolis–Hastings corrects a proposal mechanism so that the [target distribution is invariant]{.alert}
- MCMC trades independent samples for access to [complicated unnormalized densities]{.alert}
- Kernel discrepancy compares distributions and measures both [worst-case]{.alert} and [average-case integration error]{.alert}
- The kernel specifies which distributional differences and integrand features matter
- Markov chains model computational algorithms as well as dynamic systems such as queues
